terms.gloss: a nation, a people; in the genitive plural, of the nations: international
terms.grammar: noun, third declension; its genitive plural gentium serves for “international”
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.69: aliud jūs gentium, aliud jūs cīvīle
terms.comment: Latin has no adjective for “international”; it puts the nations in the genitive: jūs gentium, international law, the law the Romans held common to all peoples.

evidence: M-O s.v. international relations: necessitūdinis ratiōnēs inter populōs (Egger)
terms.comment: A description, not a word: international relations as relations between peoples.
A coinage from the modern languages, marked as such by Morgan–Owens, with multinātiōnālis and plūrinātiōnālis.

phrases.latin: Itaque majōrēs aliud jūs gentium, aliud jūs cīvīle esse voluērunt
phrases.english: So our ancestors held the law of nations to be one thing and the law of our own state another

sources: Lewis & Short: gens · Lewis & Short: inter · Lewis & Short: populus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: international; international law; international relations.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 187, 334.
